title: Education Reading Is Doing Something B. Geoghegan
author: Geoghegan, B.
summary: The author reflects on a common misconception — that reading is passive or unproductive — sparked by a conversation with someone who identified as 'more of a doer than a reader.' Several overlapping factors explain declining reading: time absorbed by screens, poor foundational literacy from the 'balanced literacy' approach adopted in the late 1980s and 1990s, and society's obsession with observable productivity. 54% of U.S. adults read below a sixth-grade level. Books change us — making us more knowledgeable, empathetic, critical, and curious — and the reader, not a visible artifact, is the product, as Emerson put it: 'I cannot remember the books I have eaten; even so, they have made me.' Reading is nourishment for the mind and soul, and reclaiming it as 'doing something' corrects a damaging false binary between action and reflection.
points: 54% of U.S. adults read below a sixth-grade level — partly a consequence of the 'balanced literacy' approach adopted in most public schools from the late 1980s onward.
Society's obsession with observable, measurable productivity is a key factor in reading's decline — the adrenaline of completing tasks crowds out the quieter gains of contemplation.
'Books change us... We are the product' — the reader, not a visible output, is transformed by reading, just as food nourishes without leaving a visible artifact.
The false dichotomy of 'doer' vs. 'reader' devalues one of the most formative activities available — reading for pleasure is itself a productive endeavor.
Our fast-paced society has moved away from valuing quiet contemplation, long walks, and front-porch conversations — and forgotten how productive those habits can be.
quotes: Someone who recently overheard me talking about my current book was intrigued and asked for other recommendations... She lamented her neglect of this habit, but attributed it to the fact that she 'wasn't much of a reader because she was more of a doer.'

Starting in the late 1980s and early 1990s, most students in the public school system were taught to read using the 'balanced literacy' approach. Critics argue that this method often failed to provide the foundational skills needed for strong reading proficiency, making reading for pleasure unlikely.

The factor that is a little harder to measure but surfaced during my conversation mentioned above is our society's obsession with busyness and productivity. I understand the adrenaline rush that comes with working hard, being productive, and completing tasks.

Books change us, making us more knowledgeable, more empathetic, more critical, or more curious. We are the 'product'. In the words of Ralph Waldo Emerson, 'I cannot remember the books I've read any more than the meals I have eaten; even so, they have made me.' No one would ever say that eating is 'unproductive'.

Over the past several decades, our fast-paced society has moved further away from valuing the benefits of quiet contemplation, long (podcast-free) walks, and front porch conversations. We've forgotten how 'productive' those habits and practices can be.
